Nuclear-Powered NASA Moon Rover Is Made of Curiosity and Perseverance Parts, Launches in 2028
11 photos
Photo: NASA
Over the past weekend, American space agency NASA laid out new plans for the conquest and colonization of the Moon. They are centered on a series of contract awards to various space companies meant to deliver increasingly more hardware to the satellite, as the Americans are racing to become the first in the world to establish an extraterrestrial outpost.
We'll get to all of that in due time, but I'll start with something that hasn't been in the news all that often: a nuclear-powered Moon rover called the Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration.
That would be PROMISE for short, a six-wheeled machine packed to the teeth with science instruments and technology demonstrations that are meant to provide us with a better understanding of the place some of us will use to live and work in the near future.
The rover is being developed by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, but not in the usual fashion, from the ground up,. Instead, engineers are using spare flight components and engineering test models that have already been used on the Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers.
This approach, says the agency, makes the development of the rover cheaper than it would have otherwise been, but also faster, as some of the parts and processes that will go into it are already available.
The PROMISE will carry with it to the Moon a drill that will help it extract regolith from some three feet (one meter) below the lunar surface, and spectrometers which it will use to analyze the material in search of ice and other resources.
It will also be equipped with temperature and radiation sensors and visible light cameras. Most importantly, though, the rover will carry to the Moon a next-gen radiation-tolerant computer, the High Performance Spaceflight Computing.
Partially autonomous, the PROMISE will be powered by a yet-undetailed nuclear system that can keep it operational in the harsh conditions of the lunar night or in the permanently shadowed regions of the Moon at the South Pole .
Aside from looking for resources that could be used to sustain a human presence there, the rover will also scout for other potential landing places for the huge number of upcoming Moon missions.
The space agency has already decided on when the rover will be launched, and who will send it to the Moon. The departure time for the PROMISE mission is the end of 2028, and the launch rocket will be a Blue Origin rocket. To get the machine down to the surface, a Mark 1 lander of the same company will be employed.
NASA will spend between $94 million and $140 million to send the rover on its way. We'll keep an eye on the mission and return with updates once more is revealed.
